answer:
**Replacing zero with the same small constant does not break symmetry.** If every hidden neuron has the same weight vector and bias, each sees the same weighted sum. If its outgoing connections are also identical, backpropagation gives each the same update. The neurons remain duplicates after every deterministic step. [1](https://www.deeplearningbook.org/contents/optimization.html)

For example, four neurons with identical weights do not initially detect four different directions in input space. They all detect one direction four times. Training has no asymmetric signal telling one to specialize differently.

A common positive constant can also accumulate many same-sign inputs, producing activation scales that grow poorly with layer width. Well-scaled random initialization addresses both diversity and signal variance.

**Randomness is a practical method, not the underlying requirement.** A deliberately designed asymmetric deterministic initialization can also work. The essential conditions are distinguishable units and suitable numerical scale. Likewise, constant biases are often fine when weights already differ. Do not infer that every parameter tensor must be random; inspect the symmetry of the whole computation and how gradients reach each unit.

**Technical details and references.**

A common nonzero constant does not break hidden-unit symmetry: neurons with identical incoming/outgoing parameters compute the same function and receive matching updates. The layer effectively wastes width. [1](https://www.deeplearningbook.org/contents/optimization.html)

It can also make activation variance grow with width because same-sign contributions accumulate. Random initialization creates distinct feature directions while controlling variance through fan-in/out scaling. There are specialized deterministic asymmetric schemes, so randomness itself is not essential; **different, appropriately scaled units** are. A constant bias can coexist with asymmetric weights without causing this problem.
